overview.title: Training with dicts, and the Functional model as an inspectable graph
overview.section: 7.2 Different ways to build Keras models
overview.main_topic: Listing 7.11 trains the ticket model with name-keyed dictionaries; then the page introduces the key advantage of Functional models, access to layer connectivity, starting with plotting the model graph via keras.utils.plot_model().
overview.central_idea: Because inputs and output layers are named, losses, metrics, inputs and targets can be passed as dictionaries keyed by those names. More generally, a Functional model is an explicit graph data structure, which lets you inspect connectivity, visualize it, and reuse intermediate nodes in new models.
overview.importance: Dict-based feeding is the robust way to handle real multi-input/output models. The 'explicit graph' property is what distinguishes the Functional API from subclassing (p.226-227) and enables the plotting and feature-extraction use cases of the next pages.
learning_objectives: Rewrite positional (list-based) compile/fit/evaluate/predict calls as name-keyed dicts.
Identify where the dictionary keys come from (the name= arguments of Input and the head layers).
Explain what it means that a Functional model is an explicit graph data structure.
Name the two use cases this enables: model visualization and feature extraction.
Use keras.utils.plot_model to draw a model's topology and read Figure 7.2.

The idea of a model as a graph of layers (p.120)

summary:
**Listing 7.11** repeats Listing 7.10 (p.222) but replaces every positional list with a dictionary keyed by names that were assigned in Listing 7.9 (p.221). In `compile()`, `loss` is `{"priority": "mean_squared_error", "department": "sparse_categorical_crossentropy"}` and `metrics` is `{"priority": ["mean_absolute_error"], "department": ["accuracy"]}`. `fit()` and `evaluate()` receive an input dict `{"title": ..., "text_body": ..., "tags": ...}` and a target dict `{"priority": ..., "department": ...}`; `predict()` receives the input dict and the two predictions are still unpacked as `priority_preds, department_preds`. Input keys match the `name=` of each `keras.Input`; output keys match the `name=` of the output layers.

Under **The power of the Functional API: Access to layer connectivity**, the authors explain that a Functional model is an *explicit graph data structure*. You can therefore *inspect how layers are connected* and *reuse previous graph nodes* (layer outputs) in new models. This matches the mental model most researchers have of a deep network: a graph of layers. Two use cases follow: **model visualization** and **feature extraction**.

**Plotting layer connectivity** begins: you can plot the topology of the model with `keras.utils.plot_model(model, "ticket_classifier.png")`. **Figure 7.2** shows the result for the ticket classifier: three `InputLayer` boxes feed a `Concatenate` box, which feeds one `Dense` box, which branches into two `Dense` boxes (the priority and department heads). The default plot shows only layer types; the next page (p.224) adds names and shapes.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Listing 7.11 trains, evaluates and runs the model using dicts of input and target arrays, plus dicts of losses and metrics, keyed by input and output names.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The mapping between data and model ports is now explicit and order-independent: "title" goes to the Input named "title", "department" to the output layer named "department", regardless of their positions in Model().
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It removes the silent-swap risk of positional lists (title_data and text_body_data have identical shapes) and documents intent in the code.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Keys of the input dict must equal the Input names; keys of the loss, metric and target dicts must equal the output layer names. predict() still returns outputs in the order of the outputs list (here a list), which is why tuple unpacking works.

paragraphs.what_it_says: A Functional model is an explicit graph; you can inspect how layers are connected and reuse previous graph nodes (layer outputs) in new models. This matches researchers' mental model of a network as a graph of layers.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Keras keeps, as data, the record of which layer was called on which tensor. That record can be queried (model.layers, layer.input, layer.output) and new models can be built from any intermediate tensor in it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Subclassed models (p.226) hide their wiring inside Python code in call(), so this inspection and reuse are not available there; it is a central reason to prefer the Functional API.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Graph nodes correspond to layer calls; their outputs are symbolic tensors that can serve as inputs or outputs of another keras.Model.

concepts.name: Functional API
concepts.definition: Model building by calling layers on symbolic tensors and wrapping inputs/outputs in keras.Model.
concepts.intuition: A wiring diagram that Keras remembers.
concepts.technical: The resulting model stores its directed acyclic graph of layer calls, which can be inspected, plotted and partially reused.
concepts.misconception: That Functional models are just a different syntax for Sequential; they can express graphs Sequential cannot and expose them as data.

concepts.name: Named inputs and outputs
concepts.definition: Inputs and output layers given a name= so data, losses and metrics can be passed as dicts keyed by name.
concepts.intuition: Labels on sockets instead of counting from the left.
concepts.technical: Keras matches dict keys to model.input_names / output layer names; mismatched keys cause errors rather than silent mistakes.
concepts.significance: Safe feeding of many-input, many-output models.
concepts.misconception: That dict keys can be the Python variable names; they must be the name= strings (here the same by choice).

concepts.name: Layer connectivity (explicit graph)
concepts.definition: The record, kept by a Functional model, of which layer outputs feed which layers.
concepts.technical: Accessible via model.layers, layer.input, layer.output; reusable to build new models from intermediate nodes.
concepts.misconception: That every Keras model has it; subclassed models do not expose an explicit graph.

pitfalls: Keys must match name= strings exactly; a typo raises a KeyError-like error.
If a layer is left unnamed, Keras auto-generates a name (e.g. dense_3), which makes dict keys awkward; name your heads.
Do not mix styles carelessly (e.g. dict losses but list targets); keep one convention.

deeper.title: Reading figure 7.2
deeper.body: From top to bottom: three `InputLayer` boxes are `title`, `text_body` and `tags`; `Concatenate` merges them into one 20,100-wide vector; the middle `Dense` is `dense_features` (64 units, relu); the two bottom `Dense` boxes are the `priority` (1 unit, sigmoid) and `department` (4 units, softmax) heads. The default plot shows only layer *types*, so the three inputs and the three Dense layers look identical; p.224 fixes this by showing names and shapes.

deeper.title: Why subclassed models cannot be plotted the same way
deeper.body: Beyond this page: a subclassed model's connectivity lives in the Python body of `call()`, which Keras cannot read as data before running it. A Functional model's connectivity is built when you call layers on symbolic tensors and then stored. The book returns to this trade-off on p.227.

misconceptions.claim: Using dicts changes how the model is trained.
misconceptions.correction: Training is identical to Listing 7.10; only the mapping between data and model ports changes.

misconceptions.claim: Dictionary keys are the Python variable names of the tensors.
misconceptions.correction: They are the name= strings given to the Inputs and output layers; the book happens to use the same strings for both.

misconceptions.claim: plot_model works on any model in the same way.
misconceptions.correction: Its usefulness comes from the explicit graph of Functional (and Sequential) models; subclassed models do not expose their internal wiring.

questions.question: In Listing 7.11, where do the keys "title", "text_body" and "tags" come from?
options: Python variable names of the arrays
The name= arguments of the keras.Input objects
The order of arguments in compile()
questions.answer: The name= arguments of the keras.Input objects
questions.explanation: Listing 7.9 created Inputs with name="title", etc. Variable names are invisible to Keras; auto-generated names would be like input_layer_1; compile() order is irrelevant for dicts.

questions.question: What two use cases does access to layer connectivity enable, according to the page?
questions.explanation: Stated directly after the explanation that a Functional model is an explicit graph data structure.

questions.question: What does it mean that a Functional model is an 'explicit graph data structure', and what can you do with it?
questions.answer: Keras stores which layer is applied to which tensors, so you can inspect how layers are connected and reuse earlier graph nodes (layer outputs) as parts of new models.
questions.explanation: The book highlights inspection and reuse of previous graph nodes; this also matches the researcher's mental model of a network as a graph of layers.

questions.question: In Figure 7.2, what does the single Dense box between Concatenate and the two bottom Dense boxes correspond to?
questions.explanation: Listing 7.9 passes the concatenated features through Dense(64, relu, name="dense_features"), which then feeds both heads. The heads are the two bottom boxes; inputs are at the top.

questions.question: Give one advantage of the dict style of Listing 7.11 over the list style of Listing 7.10 for this specific model.
questions.answer: title_data and text_body_data have the same shape, so a positional swap would go unnoticed; with dicts each array is explicitly bound to its named input.
questions.explanation: The book motivates dicts by not wanting to rely on input order, e.g. with many inputs or outputs.
